conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. My goal is to understand how you’re doing so we can make sure you have the support you deserve. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one, and you can answer in your own words. Shall we begin?

1. In the past week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy, I’ll catch myself giggling. It’s not every moment, but the funny side of things hasn’t disappeared.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—like when my little guy lets out a huge burp right after I finish feeding him, I can’t help but crack up. It might take me a second to notice the humor, but it’s definitely still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to stuff—like tomorrow morning I’m planning to take the baby out in the stroller to the park, and I’m actually excited about getting a coffee on the way. It feels nice to have little things to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby spits up a ton or won’t settle, I might think, “Maybe I ate something that bothered him,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies are just unpredictable, and tomorrow’s a new day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if he’s breathing okay when he’s napping, even though the monitor looks fine. It’s quick—like a little jolt—then I peek in and feel silly for worrying. It’s not all day, just random moments.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicked feeling—just the quick “is he okay?” worry, then it passes. Nothing that makes my heart race or feels like real fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of nights ago the dishes were piled up, the baby wouldn’t go down, and I thought, “I can’t do everything.” But once he finally slept and I cleared the sink, I felt back on track. It’s momentary, not a constant weight.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping pretty well—usually get a four-hour stretch, then a couple of two-hour chunks. I’m tired from the night feeds, but I drift off again once he’s settled.
I have felt sad or miserable

I wouldn’t call it miserable—more like a brief “blah” if the day feels long. Yesterday evening I got a bit teary when I couldn’t soothe him quickly, but five minutes later he smiled at me and the sadness lifted.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t had any of those big, can’t-stop crying spells. Maybe just a couple of tears when I was overtired the other night, but nothing overwhelming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You're doing a beautiful job navigating the early weeks with your baby. From what you've shared-still giggling at your little one's funny moments, looking forward to stroller walks, and bouncing back quickly after brief moments of worry or fatigue-it sounds like you're adjusting well overall. It's completely natural to have the occasional <sym>anxious jolt</sym> when you check his breathing or to feel a bit <sym>overwhelmed</sym> when dishes pile up, yet you've been able to soothe yourself and move forward with resilience.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries about infant safety without objective cause, occurring "sometimes" and causing distress</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your EPDS total of 7 sits below the 8-point threshold, indicating that <med>major postpartum depression</med> is unlikely at this time. You report preserved enjoyment (<quote>excited about getting a coffee</quote>), intact sleep, and no persistent low mood, <sym>guilt</sym>, or <sym>panic</sym>. Occasional <sym>worry</sym> and brief <sym>tearfulness</sym> are common postpartum adjustment symptoms and do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which requires ≥5 symptoms (including either depressed mood or loss of interest) for two weeks, plus clinically significant distress. Your answers show only two mild items: fleeting <sym>anxiety</sym> (Q4 score 2) and minor <sym>sadness</sym> (Q8-9 score 1 each). No self-harm ideation was endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and re-screen at the next visit or sooner if symptoms escalate
2. Practice quick grounding techniques (deep breaths, shoulder roll-outs) when the <sym>breathing-check worry</sym> pops up
3. Keep scheduling small outings like the <quote>stroller and coffee</quote> to maintain positive anticipation
4. Share any persistent low mood, <sym>panic</sym>, or thoughts of self-harm immediately with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med>
5. Lean on your support network-partner, family, or local new-parent groups-for reassurance and practical help
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Self-report on 10-item EPDS-equivalent questionnaire, 2–3 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms endorsed  
– Fleeting anxious thoughts about infant safety (Q4) – brief, situational, no panic.  
– Transient feeling “blah” / brief tearfulness when infant is hard to soothe (Q8, Q9) – resolves quickly.  
– Occasional sense of being momentarily overwhelmed (Q6) – situational, recovers same day.

Symptoms denied  
Loss of pleasure or laughter (Q1, Q2), persistent sadness or crying spells (Q7–9), guilt/self-blame (Q3), panic (Q5), sleep disturbance linked to mood (Q7), self-harm ideation (Q10).

Pattern summary  
No sustained low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, or neuro-vegetative symptoms. Intermittent, mild worry and situational frustration only.

Screening significance  
Current responses place overall score below standard cut-off for probable major postpartum depression; isolated mild anxiety symptoms noted. No current safety concerns (zero self-harm ideation). Continue routine care and re-screen at next postpartum visit or sooner if symptoms escalate.
